entries.prompt: What engineers actually do all day: how engineering careers really work, from the first job and the first failure to leading a team, told by working engineers

tapeRelevanceAnchors.claim: The credentialing path into engineering work can wind through degrees that aren't engineering at all — a chemistry bachelor's, a textile-chemistry master's, and a PhD in fiber and polymer science feeding straight into an engineering-adjacent career.
Joe Couitt's first job in manufacturing, handed to him by his machinist father the year he turned eighteen, was mopping floors — not running a single machine.
David Oh didn't know what engineering even was until he got to college; growing up with two doctor parents in Birmingham, all he knew was that he loved space and was good at science and math.

After tracing an inconsistent press result back to a single slipped locating pin, Daniel Servansky didn't stop at fixing that one part — he built new go/no-go gauges and a preventative-maintenance task specifically so that failure mode could never happen again on that line.
Joel Williams argues that pointing out risk is rarely rewarded compared to finding opportunity — except in safety-critical work like airplane design, where a risk mindset is non-negotiable.

Ian McEachern, whose kinetic sculptures have landed in Times Square, Walt Disney World, and the Smithsonian, learned that even that kind of work only keeps getting built once it is tied to a client's revenue, not made purely for its own sake.
Krishna Raichur describes reduced-order simulation models that run in seconds against live sensor data, letting an engineer spot overheating and schedule maintenance before a machine actually fails.
Rick James spent twenty-five years working as a mechanical and electrical engineer before founding SimuTech Group and building it into ANSYS's number-one reseller partner in North America.

Pat Stephens moved from a product-development engineering role at Gore, through Boston Scientific and Medtronic, to VP of R&D at Shockwave Medical, where her team builds balloon catheters that use acoustic waves to break up calcification inside arteries.
Dylan Lundberg describes automation turning modern milling floors into button-pushing and simple loading, against a traditional mill shop where a single machinist babysits just one or two molds.
